overview: East Saxon kingship, London commerce and changing religious patronage are recorded by Bede. The elite burial at Prittlewell adds evidence for music, craftsmanship and long-distance connections, but does not securely identify a named king.

items.text: Radiocarbon evidence and Frankish coins place the Prittlewell burial between about 580 and 605. This interval crosses 597, so it cannot by itself prove burial before Augustine arrived.
Gold foil crosses were placed near the coffin head. They support a Christian interpretation of this elite burial without identifying its occupant.
A lyre with garnet fittings and vessels linked to the eastern Mediterranean connect the burial to skilled music-making and far-reaching exchange.

Bede places Mellitus among the East Saxons in 604 and describes King Saeberht as subject to his uncle, King Aethelberht of Kent. This is a reported overlordship relationship, not a modern national boundary.
Bede describes London as a trading centre reached by land and sea and credits Aethelberht with building St Paul's for its bishop.

After Saeberht died, Bede reports that his sons rejected the bishop and Mellitus departed. His partisan church history documents a reversal of patronage, not the disappearance of the East Saxon kingdom.

sources.title: Bede, Ecclesiastical History, translated A. M. Sellar
